claim: Ankyrins together with their spectrin partners are the master organizers of micron-scale membrane domains in diverse tissues.
source: Ankyrins together with their spectrin partners are the master organizers of micron-scale membrane domains in diverse tissues.
evidence: This is a general statement about ankyrin function presented in the abstract without specific experimental data in this manuscript, but draws from established scientific understanding.

claim: The 24 ankyrin (ANK) repeats of ankyrins bind to numerous membrane proteins, linking them to spectrin-based cytoskeletons at specific membrane microdomains.
source: The 24 ankyrin (ANK) repeats of ankyrins bind to numerous membrane proteins, linking them to spectrin-based cytoskeletons at specific membrane microdomains.
evidence: This is a statement about the known function of ANK repeats, drawing from established knowledge in the field.

claim: The entire ANK repeats of ankyrin-B/G are inhibited by combinatorial and quasi-independent bindings of multiple disordered segments located in the ankyrin-B/G linkers and tails.
source: We discovered that the entire ANK repeats are inhibited by combinatorial and quasi-independent bindings of multiple disordered segments located in the ankyrin-B/G linkers and tails, suggesting a mechanistic basis for differential regulations of membrane target bindings by ankyrins.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by biochemical, biophysical, and structural data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Mutations of ankyrins are associated with hereditary spherocytosis.
source: Mutations of ankyrins are known to be associated with various diseases in humans such as hereditary spherocytosis (Eber et al., 1996; Lux et al., 1990; Gallagher, 2005), cardiac arrhythmia syndromes and sinus node dysfunction (Mohler et al., 2003; Mohler et al., 2007; Le Scouarnec et al., 2008; Hashemi et al., 2009), bipolar disorders (Baum et al., 2008; Ferreira et al., 2008; Schulze et al., 2009; Scott et al., 2009; Takata et al., 2011; Dedman et al., 2012; Rueckert et al., 2013), schizophrenia (Nie et al., 2015; Ripke et al., 2011) and autism spectrum disorder (Willsey et al., 2013; Parikshak et al., 2013; Shi et al., 2013; Iqbal et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple literature citations.

claim: Mutations of ankyrins are associated with cardiac arrhythmia syndromes and sinus node dysfunction.
source: Mutations of ankyrins are known to be associated with various diseases in humans such as hereditary spherocytosis (Eber et al., 1996; Lux et al., 1990; Gallagher, 2005), cardiac arrhythmia syndromes and sinus node dysfunction (Mohler et al., 2003; Mohler et al., 2007; Le Scouarnec et al., 2008; Hashemi et al., 2009), bipolar disorders (Baum et al., 2008; Ferreira et al., 2008; Schulze et al., 2009; Scott et al., 2009; Takata et al., 2011; Dedman et al., 2012; Rueckert et al., 2013), schizophrenia (Nie et al., 2015; Ripke et al., 2011) and autism spectrum disorder (Willsey et al., 2013; Parikshak et al., 2013; Shi et al., 2013; Iqbal et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple literature citations.

claim: Mutations of ankyrins are associated with bipolar disorders.
source: Mutations of ankyrins are known to be associated with various diseases in humans such as hereditary spherocytosis (Eber et al., 1996; Lux et al., 1990; Gallagher, 2005), cardiac arrhythmia syndromes and sinus node dysfunction (Mohler et al., 2003; Mohler et al., 2007; Le Scouarnec et al., 2008; Hashemi et al., 2009), bipolar disorders (Baum et al., 2008; Ferreira et al., 2008; Schulze et al., 2009; Scott et al., 2009; Takata et al., 2011; Dedman et al., 2012; Rueckert et al., 2013), schizophrenia (Nie et al., 2015; Ripke et al., 2011) and autism spectrum disorder (Willsey et al., 2013; Parikshak et al., 2013; Shi et al., 2013; Iqbal et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple literature citations.

claim: Mutations of ankyrins are associated with schizophrenia.
source: Mutations of ankyrins are known to be associated with various diseases in humans such as hereditary spherocytosis (Eber et al., 1996; Lux et al., 1990; Gallagher, 2005), cardiac arrhythmia syndromes and sinus node dysfunction (Mohler et al., 2003; Mohler et al., 2007; Le Scouarnec et al., 2008; Hashemi et al., 2009), bipolar disorders (Baum et al., 2008; Ferreira et al., 2008; Schulze et al., 2009; Scott et al., 2009; Takata et al., 2011; Dedman et al., 2012; Rueckert et al., 2013), schizophrenia (Nie et al., 2015; Ripke et al., 2011) and autism spectrum disorder (Willsey et al., 2013; Parikshak et al., 2013; Shi et al., 2013; Iqbal et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple literature citations.

claim: Mutations of ankyrins are associated with autism spectrum disorder.
source: Mutations of ankyrins are known to be associated with various diseases in humans such as hereditary spherocytosis (Eber et al., 1996; Lux et al., 1990; Gallagher, 2005), cardiac arrhythmia syndromes and sinus node dysfunction (Mohler et al., 2003; Mohler et al., 2007; Le Scouarnec et al., 2008; Hashemi et al., 2009), bipolar disorders (Baum et al., 2008; Ferreira et al., 2008; Schulze et al., 2009; Scott et al., 2009; Takata et al., 2011; Dedman et al., 2012; Rueckert et al., 2013), schizophrenia (Nie et al., 2015; Ripke et al., 2011) and autism spectrum disorder (Willsey et al., 2013; Parikshak et al., 2013; Shi et al., 2013; Iqbal et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple literature citations.

claim: The ankyrin family in vertebrates consists of three members: ankyrin-R (AnkR), ankyrin-B (AnkB) and ankyrin-G (AnkG).
source: In vertebrates, the ankyrin family consists of three members: ankyrin-R (AnkR), ankyrin-B (AnkB) and ankyrin-G (AnkG).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the ankyrin family composition in vertebrates.

claim: AnkR, AnkB, and AnkG share similar domain organizations but usually locate at different subcellular regions and perform divergent physiological functions.
source: They share similar domain organizations (Figure 1A), but usually locate at different subcellular regions and perform divergent physiological functions (Mohler et al., 2002; Abdi et al., 2006; He et al., 2013; Bennett and Lorenzo, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and reference to Figure 1A showing domain organization.

claim: Each ankyrin contains an N-terminal membrane binding domain (MBD) composed of 24 ANK repeats responsible for binding to diverse membrane targets.
source: Each ankyrin contains an N-terminal membrane binding domain (MBD), which is composed of 24 ANK repeats and responsible for binding to diverse membrane targets.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ankyrin structure and function.

claim: The 24 ANK repeats of ankyrins are among the longest extended repeat-containing domains in living organisms.
source: The 24 ANK repeats of ankyrins are among the longest extended repeat-containing domains in living organisms.
evidence: This is a comparative statement about the length of ANK repeats relative to other repeat-containing domains, drawing from established knowledge.

claim: Long repeat-containing proteins form long solenoid structures with high conformational plasticity.
source: A trademark of long repeat-containing proteins is their formations of long solenoid structures with high conformational plasticity (Lee et al., 2006b; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Following the MBD is an unstructured linker region of ~130 amino acid residues.
source: Following the MBD is an unstructured linker region of ~130 amino acid residues, followed sequentially by a ZU5-ZU5-UPA supramodule responsible for spectrin binding (SBD) (Mohler et al., 2004a; Wang et al., 2012), a death domain (DD), and an intrinsically disordered C-terminal tail (CT) with varying lengths (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a structural description supported by reference to Figure 1A and citations.

claim: The ZU5-ZU5-UPA supramodule is responsible for spectrin binding (SBD).
source: Following the MBD is an unstructured linker region of ~130 amino acid residues, followed sequentially by a ZU5-ZU5-UPA supramodule responsible for spectrin binding (SBD) (Mohler et al., 2004a; Wang et al., 2012), a death domain (DD), and an intrinsically disordered C-terminal tail (CT) with varying lengths (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The folded structural domains (MBD, SBD and DD) in ankyrins share very high sequence similarities.
source: The folded structural domains (i.e. MBD, SBD and DD) in ankyrins share very high sequence similarities (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1A which shows sequence identities.

claim: The unstructured regions of ankyrins (linker region and CT) are more divergent among family members than the folded structural domains.
source: In contrast, the unstructured regions of ankyrins (i.e. the linker region and CT), although fairly conserved within each isoform, are more divergent among the family members (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1A showing sequence comparisons.

claim: The isoform-specific unstructured linker and tail regions are largely responsible for distinct functions of each member of the ankyrin family proteins.
source: Presumably, these isoform-specific and unstructured linker and tail regions are largely responsible for distinct functions of each member of the ankyrin family proteins (see Abdi et al., 2006 and He et al., 2013 for examples).
evidence: This is a speculative statement ('presumably') supported by citations to examples in the literature.

claim: Ankyrin is an ancient molecule that appeared as early as in bilaterians over 500 million years ago.
source: Ankyrin is an ancient molecule that appeared as early as in bilaterians over 500 million years ago (Cai and Zhang, 2006; Bennett and Lorenzo, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The 24 ANK repeats of ankyrins have retained a remarkable level of amino acid sequence conservation throughout evolution.
source: The 24 ANK repeats of ankyrins have retained a remarkable level of amino acid sequence conservation throughout the evolution, and different ANK repeats binding membrane proteins with diverse sequences have evolved at different stages of the evolution (Hill et al., 2008; Bennett and Lorenzo, 2013; Bennett and Lorenzo, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Different ANK repeats binding membrane proteins with diverse sequences have evolved at different stages of evolution.
source: The 24 ANK repeats of ankyrins have retained a remarkable level of amino acid sequence conservation throughout the evolution, and different ANK repeats binding membrane proteins with diverse sequences have evolved at different stages of the evolution (Hill et al., 2008; Bennett and Lorenzo, 2013; Bennett and Lorenzo, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The highly conserved 24 ANK repeats can form multiple semi-independent target binding sites, each capable of recognizing short and intrinsically disordered segments with variable amino acid sequences distributed on target proteins.
source: In an earlier study, we demonstrated that the highly conserved 24 ANK repeats can form multiple semi-independent target binding sites, and each capable of recognizing short and intrinsically disordered segments with variable amino acid sequences distributed on target proteins (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' prior work.

claim: ANK repeats are capable of binding to a very diverse array of target proteins with high specificity.
source: As such, ANK repeats are capable of binding to a very diverse array of target proteins with high specificity, a strategy that may be commonly employed by long repeat-containing scaffold proteins (Wang et al., 2014; Chook and Blobel, 2001; Conti et al., 1998; Graham et al., 2000; Huber and Weis, 2001; Kobe, 1999; Xu et al., 2010; Zhu et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The target bindings of ankyrin's ANK repeats must be regulated during the biogenesis and trafficking processes of ankyrins and their targets.
source: The target bindings of ankyrin's ANK repeats must be regulated during the biogenesis and trafficking processes of ankyrins and their targets, as otherwise functionally unrelated membrane targets would be misdirected to the same sites in cellular membranes.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the need to prevent misdirection of membrane targets.

claim: The formation of each ankyrin/target complex at specific membrane domains needs to be regulated to fulfill excitation/resting cycles of excitable tissues such as neurons and muscles.
source: Additionally, the formation of each ankyrin/target complex (e.g. the ankyrin-B/G and sodium channel complexes) at specific membrane domains also needs to be regulated to fulfill excitation/resting cycles of excitable tissues such as neurons and muscles (Bréchet et al., 2008; Garver et al., 1997; Whittard et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Earlier studies have suggested that ankyrins can adopt autoinhibited conformation by using sequences outside the ANK repeats to directly interact with the repeats to regulate their target bindings.
source: Earlier studies have suggested that ankyrins can adopt autoinhibited conformation (i.e. by using sequences outside the ANK repeats to directly interact with the repeats) to regulate their target bindings (Abdi et al., 2006; Davis et al., 1992; He et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2014), but the mechanisms of the autoinhibition are unknown.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Three distinct autoinhibitory segments from the intrinsically disordered linker and CT regions of AnkB were identified.
source: In this study, we systematically investigated the autoinhibition mechanisms of ANK repeats of ankyrin-B and G (AnkB and G). We identified three distinct autoinhibitory segments from the intrinsically disordered linker and CT regions of AnkB, and elucidated the inhibition mechanism of these segments by detailed biochemical and structural investigations.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by biochemical and structural data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The three inhibitory segments of AnkB spread along the entire 24 ANK repeats and bind to the repeats in a quasi-independent manner.
source: Our study reveals that the three inhibitory segments spread along the entire 24 ANK repeats and bind to the repeats in a quasi-independent manner, so that the inhibitory sites may be combinatorially regulated in response to different binding targets.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by biochemical and structural data.

claim: AnkG adopts a similar overall autoinhibition strategy as AnkB does, but with its own unique binding features.
source: We further demonstrated that AnkG also adopts a similar overall autoinhibition strategy as AnkB does, but with its own unique binding features.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by biochemical data presented in the manuscript.

claim: AnkB and AnkG contain a 13-residue segment (AI-a) that shares a similar sequence pattern with the last 13-residue fragment of AnkR_CT and several MBD 'site-1' binding targets.
source: Although AnkB and G do not contain AnkR_CT like sequences in their tails, more thorough sequence analysis revealed that both AnkB and G contain a 13-residue segment (denoted as 'AI-a' for the AutoInhibition segment-a, Figure 1A) that share a similar sequence pattern with the last 13-residue fragment of AnkR_CT and several MBD 'site-1' binding targets such as Na+ and K+-channels (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The 13-residue AI-a fragment is almost completely conserved in AnkB and AnkG among vertebrates.
source: This 13-resdiue AI-a fragment is almost completely conserved in AnkB and AnkG among vertebrates (alignments not shown).
evidence: This claim is based on sequence analysis performed by the authors.

claim: A Glu residue corresponding to Glu1622 in AnkR_CT and Glu1112 in Nav1.2, which is absolutely required for AnkR_CT and Nav1.2 to bind to ANK repeats, is invariant in AnkB and G.
source: Importantly, a Glu residue corresponding to Glu1622 in AnkR_CT and Glu1112 in Nav1.2, which has been shown to be absolutely required for AnkR_CT and Nav1.2 to bind to ANK repeats (Mohler et al., 2004b; Wang et al., 2014), is also invariant in AnkB and G (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 1B and citations to prior literature.

claim: A peptide encompassing AnkB_AI-a segment binds to AnkB ANK repeats with a dissociation constant (Kd) ~7.3 μM.
source: We found that a peptide encompassing this AnkB_AI-a segment binds to AnkB ANK repeats with a dissociation constant (Kd) ~7.3 μM based on a fluorescence polarization binding assay (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence polarization binding assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Point mutations of the positively charged residues in repeat 1 (R1) of ANK repeats (37RAAR40 to 37EAAE40) of AnkB significantly decreased its binding to the AI-a peptide.
source: Point mutations of the positively charged residues in the repeat 1 (R1) of ANK repeats (37RAAR40 to 37EAAE40) of AnkB significantly decreased its binding to the AI-a peptide (Figure 1C), consistent with our previous structural analysis that the positively charged residues in the ANK repeat R1 play a role in binding to the negatively charged residues from the 'site-1'-binding peptides.
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence polarization binding assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The AnkR/B_CT Chimera peptide binds to AnkB_MBD with a Kd value comparable to that of AnkR_CT with AnkB_MBD.
source: Isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) experiments detected a strong interaction between this chimera peptide and AnkB_MBD, with a Kd value comparable to that of AnkR_CT with AnkB_MBD (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The structure of the AnkR/B_CT Chimera/AnkB_repeats_R1-20 fusion protein was determined at 3.3 Å resolution.
source: With this strategy, we successfully obtained crystals of the AnkR/B_CT Chimera/AnkB_repeats_R1-20 fusion protein, and the crystals were diffracted up to 3.3 Å.
evidence: This is a structural determination reported in the study.

claim: The AnkB_AI-a segment binds to 'site-1' of AnkB_MBD (repeats_R1-5) using essentially the same binding mode as observed in the AnkR_CT/AnkB_MBD and Nav1.2_ABD/AnkB_R1-9 complex structures.
source: Consistent with the biochemical analysis, the structure showed that the AnkB_AI-a segment binds to 'site-1' of AnkB_MBD (repeats_R1-5) using essentially the same binding mode as we observed in the AnkR_CT/AnkB_MBD and Nav1.2_ABD/AnkB_R1-9 complex structures (Wang et al., 2014) (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 1F and comparison to prior structures.

claim: Glu1630 from AnkB_AI-a occupies the identical position as Glu1622 in AnkR or Glu1112 in Nav1.2 on AnkB_R1-5, forming strong hydrogen bonds with Thr94 and Asn98 in the R2-R3 finger loop.
source: In particular, Glu1630 from AnkB_AI-a occupies the identical position as Glu1622 in AnkR or Glu1112 in Nav1.2 on AnkB_R1-5, by forming strong hydrogen bonds with Thr94 and Asn98 in the R2-R3 finger loop (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Hydrophobic interactions between 'PPIV' from AI-a and hydrophobic residues from R3-R5 contribute to the binding.
source: Additionally, hydrophobic interactions between 'PPIV' from AI-a and hydrophobic residues (including the two critical Phe residues, Phe131 and Phe164, from R4 and R5; see Wang et al., 2014) from R3-R5 also contribute to the binding (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The amino acid sequences of the linker connecting MBD and SBD within each isoform of ankyrins are highly conserved.
source: Though the conservation among the three isoforms is limited, the amino acid sequences of the linker connecting MBD and SBD within each isoform of ankyrins are highly conserved (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence comparison shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The crystal structure of AnkR MBD C-terminal 12 ANK repeats (PDB ID: 1N11) contains a 14-residue fragment of the linker that folds back and binds to the last five repeats (R20-24) of MBD.
source: The crystal structure of AnkR MBD C-terminal 12 ANK repeats (PDB ID: 1N11, referred to as AnkR_C12) contains a 14-residue fragment of the linker that folds back and binds to the last five repeats (R20-24) of MBD (Michaely et al., 2002) (also see below for more details).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior structural study.

claim: The linker region of AnkB directly interacts with MBD, preventing AnkB from localizing to plasma membranes.
source: Recently, the linker region of AnkB was reported to directly interact with MBD, thus preventing AnkB from localizing to plasma membranes (He et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Extending the linker region from residue 847 to 965 (AnkB 28–847 vs AnkB 28–965) led to weakened or complete loss of interactions between MBD and three target proteins (Nav1.2, E-cadherin, and NF186/L1CAM).
source: Interestingly, extending the linker region from residue 847 to 965 (AnkB 28–847 vs AnkB 28–965) invariably led to weakened or completely loss of interactions between MBD and the three target proteins (Figure 2B and C), indicating that an additional segment within the residues 848–965 can bind to the ANK repeats of AnkB and acts as another autoinhibitory sequence.
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC binding data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: An additional segment within residues 848–965 can bind to the ANK repeats of AnkB and acts as another autoinhibitory sequence.
source: Interestingly, extending the linker region from residue 847 to 965 (AnkB 28–847 vs AnkB 28–965) invariably led to weakened or completely loss of interactions between MBD and the three target proteins (Figure 2B and C), indicating that an additional segment within the residues 848–965 can bind to the ANK repeats of AnkB and acts as another autoinhibitory sequence.
evidence: This is an inference based on the binding data showing that extending the linker weakens target binding.

claim: Including the AI-a fragment in the MBD extension (AnkB ΔZZUD) further eliminated the remaining binding of Nav1.2.
source: Including the AI-a fragment in the MBD extension (AnkB ΔZZUD) further eliminated the remaining binding of Nav1.2 (Figure 2B and C), and this is consistent with our findings that AI-a and Nav1.2 bind to R1-5 of MBD in a mutually competitive manner (Figure 1F; and Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC binding data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: The entire linker (aa 828–965) binds to AnkB ANK repeats only (aa 28–827) with a Kd about 0.044 μM.
source: We confirmed the direct interaction between the entire linker (aa 828–965) with the AnkB ANK repeats only (aa 28–827) using an ITC-based binding assay, and data showed a strong binding (Kd about 0.044 μM, Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC binding data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The entire linker (aa 828–965) binds to AnkB 28–847 with a Kd ~4.2 μM.
source: The entire linker (aa 828–965) was found to bind to AnkB 28–847 with a Kd ~4.2 μM (Figure 2E), further indicating that a fragment within residues 848–965 can directly bind to AnkB_MBD.
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC binding data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: AnkB 28–873 interacts with the entire linker (aa 828–965) with a similar affinity as AnkB 28–847 does.
source: Another version of extended MBD, AnkB 28–873 interacts with the entire linker (aa 828–965) with a similar affinity as AnkB 28–847 does (Figure 2F), suggesting that residue 848–873 has marginal impact on the AnkB autoinhibition.
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC binding data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Residues 848–873 have marginal impact on AnkB autoinhibition.
source: Another version of extended MBD, AnkB 28–873 interacts with the entire linker (aa 828–965) with a similar affinity as AnkB 28–847 does (Figure 2F), suggesting that residue 848–873 has marginal impact on the AnkB autoinhibition.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similar binding affinities observed in ITC experiments.

claim: The AnkB linker region contains two discrete autoinhibitory segments: AI-b within region 848–965 binding to middle repeats of AnkB_MBD, and AI-c within residues 828–847.
source: Taken together, the above biochemical mapping experiments suggested that the AnkB linker region contains two discrete autoinhibitory segments: one segment within the region 848–965 binding to middle repeats of AnkB_MBD (denoted as AI-b), and the other within residues 828–847 overlapping with the short 14-residue segment observed in the AnkR_C12 structure (denoted as AI-c) (Figure 2A; and see below for further detailed mapping).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the biochemical mapping experiments presented in the study.

claim: AI-b was mapped to a 32-aa fragment (aa 865–896) from the linker.
source: First, we mapped the minimal regions of AI-b and the corresponding repeats from MBD responsible for the interaction. Using the scheme described in Figure 2E as the assay, we mapped AI-b to a 32-aa fragment (aa 865–896) from the linker (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC-based mapping data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The AI-b binding region was mapped to R6-14 of MBD.
source: Using a similar approach combined with truncations of various repeats, we mapped the AI-b binding regions to R6-14 of MBD (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC-based mapping data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The crystal structure of AnkB repeats 8–14 fused to the C-terminus of AnkB_AI-b (aa 857–896) was determined at 2.35 Å resolution.
source: We determined the crystal structure of AnkB repeats 8–14 fused to the C-terminus of AnkB_AI-b (aa 857–896) at 2.35 Å resolution (Table 1).
evidence: This is a structural determination reported in the study.

claim: The AI-b peptide binds to the inner groove formed by repeats 10–13.
source: The AI-b peptide binds to the inner groove formed by repeats 10–13 (Figure 3C), covering a large portion of the target binding 'site-3' (repeats 11–14) and a small portion of 'site-2' (repeats 7–10) that were defined in our previous study (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The AI-b autoinhibitory interaction partially inhibits the binding of Nav1.2 and NF186 to MBD.
source: The structure is also consistent with our biochemical data that the autoinhibitory interaction mediated by AI-b partially inhibits the binding of Nav1.2 and NF186 to MBD (Figure 2B), as both targets use the 'site-3' of MBD as one of the binding sites (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural data and biochemical binding data.

claim: Substitutions of hydrophobic residues within 'site-3' with Gln (Leu366Gln, Phe399Gln, and Leu432Gln) completely disrupted AI-b's binding to MBD.
source: Consistent with this observation, substitutions of hydrophobic residues within the 'site-3' with Gln (Leu366Gln, Phe399Gln, and Leu432Gln) completely disrupted AI-b's binding to MBD, and substitutions of hydrophobic residues within the 'site-2' with Gln (Ile267Gln, Leu300Gln) mildly weakened the AI-b/MBD interaction (Figure 3E; see Wang et al., 2014 for the rational of the mutations).
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC binding data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Substitutions of hydrophobic residues within 'site-2' with Gln (Ile267Gln, Leu300Gln) mildly weakened the AI-b/MBD interaction.
source: Consistent with this observation, substitutions of hydrophobic residues within the 'site-3' with Gln (Leu366Gln, Phe399Gln, and Leu432Gln) completely disrupted AI-b's binding to MBD, and substitutions of hydrophobic residues within the 'site-2' with Gln (Ile267Gln, Leu300Gln) mildly weakened the AI-b/MBD interaction (Figure 3E; see Wang et al., 2014 for the rational of the mutations).
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC binding data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The electron densities of the MBD_R8-14 bound AI-b only allowed tracing of residues spanning Gly883-Glu892.
source: The electron densities of the MBD_R8-14 bound AI-b only allowed us to trace residues spanning Gly883-Glu892 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a description of the structural data obtained from crystallography.

claim: Residues Glu865-Asp882 directly participate in binding to MBD_R8-14, as deletion of residues from 865 to 873 significantly weakened AI-b's binding to AnkB_MBD.
source: Although residues Glu865-Asp882 could not be traced in the crystal structure, this segment also directly participates in binding to MBD_R8-14, as deletion of residues from 865 to 873 significantly weakened AI-b's binding to AnkB_MBD (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an inference based on deletion mutagenesis data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Tyr886 forms a hydrogen bond with His374 and hydrophobic interactions with Phe399 and Ile404.
source: The structure of the MBD_R8-14/AI-b complex reveals their binding details: Tyr886 forms a hydrogen bond with His374 and hydrophobic interactions with Phe399 and Ile404; Met884 inserts into a hydrophobic pocket formed by Lys407, Val437, Phe440 and Met441; and Arg888 forms a number of hydrogen bonds with the sidechain of Tyr365 and backbone of Leu363 as well as charge-charge interaction with Asp364 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Met884 inserts into a hydrophobic pocket formed by Lys407, Val437, Phe440 and Met441.
source: The structure of the MBD_R8-14/AI-b complex reveals their binding details: Tyr886 forms a hydrogen bond with His374 and hydrophobic interactions with Phe399 and Ile404; Met884 inserts into a hydrophobic pocket formed by Lys407, Val437, Phe440 and Met441; and Arg888 forms a number of hydrogen bonds with the sidechain of Tyr365 and backbone of Leu363 as well as charge-charge interaction with Asp364 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Arg888 forms hydrogen bonds with the sidechain of Tyr365 and backbone of Leu363 as well as charge-charge interaction with Asp364.
source: The structure of the MBD_R8-14/AI-b complex reveals their binding details: Tyr886 forms a hydrogen bond with His374 and hydrophobic interactions with Phe399 and Ile404; Met884 inserts into a hydrophobic pocket formed by Lys407, Val437, Phe440 and Met441; and Arg888 forms a number of hydrogen bonds with the sidechain of Tyr365 and backbone of Leu363 as well as charge-charge interaction with Asp364 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Single point substitution of Tyr886 from AI-b with Ala significantly decreased its binding to MBD.
source: ITC results showed that single point substitution of Tyr886 from AI-b with Ala significantly decreased its binding to MBD, and Met884Ala, Tyr886Ala double mutations totally abolished the AI-b's autoinhibition (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC binding data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Met884Ala, Tyr886Ala double mutations totally abolished AI-b's autoinhibition.
source: ITC results showed that single point substitution of Tyr886 from AI-b with Ala significantly decreased its binding to MBD, and Met884Ala, Tyr886Ala double mutations totally abolished the AI-b's autoinhibition (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC binding data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Met884 in AI-b occupies the same hydrophobic pocket as Ile1588 in AnkR_CT does.
source: It is noted that Met884 in AI-b occupies the same hydrophobic pocket as Ile1588 in AnkR_CT does, although the two 'site-3' binding fragments share very little amino acid sequence similarity (Figure 3F), further highlighting the remarkable capacity of ANK repeats in binding to targets with diverse amino acid sequences (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 3F.

claim: A longer region of the linker (828–849 in human AnkB) is highly conserved in all three isoforms of ankyrins.
source: A longer region of the linker (i.e. 828–849 in human AnkB) is highly conserved in all three isoforms of ankyrins (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The crystal structure of AnkB C-terminal 12 repeats-linker (aa 430–873) was solved at 1.95 Å resolution.
source: To ensure that we do not miss any possible residues forming the AI-c binding segment, we prepared a C-terminal 12 ANK repeats of AnkB followed by a 46-residue linker (aa 430–873), which covers a small part of AI-b (Figure 3A), and solved the crystal structure of the protein at 1.95 Å resolution (Table 1).
evidence: This is a structural determination reported in the study.

claim: The overall structure of AnkB C-terminal 12 repeats-linker is very similar to that of AnkR_C12 (RMSD of 1.04 Å).
source: The overall structure of our AnkB C-terminal 12 repeats-linker is very similar to that of AnkR_C12 (RMSD of 1.04 Å, Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The AnkB structure contains a longer linker folded back binding to the AnkB ANK repeats, with a 20-residue linker (from Thr828 to Asp847) clearly defined.
source: However, our structure contains a longer linker folded back binding to the AnkB ANK repeats. A 20-residue linker (from Thr828 to Asp847 instead of 11 residues in AnkR_C12) is clearly defined, and this 20-residue linker extends to the repeat R18 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: A prominently positive-charged surface exists in the inner groove of R16-18 right next to Asp847.
source: Moreover, we observed a prominently positive-charged surface in the inner groove of R16-18 right next to Asp847, and the five residues following Asp847 are highly negatively charged and conserved (847DEEGDD852) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data and charge potential surface analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The five residues following Asp847 are highly negatively charged and conserved (847DEEGDD852).
source: Moreover, we observed a prominently positive-charged surface in the inner groove of R16-18 right next to Asp847, and the five residues following Asp847 are highly negatively charged and conserved (847DEEGDD852) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis and structural data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The stretch of negatively charged residues 847DEEGDD852 is anticipated to be part of AI-c and involved in binding to MBD (likely R16-17).
source: We anticipate that this stretch of negatively charged residues is part of AI-c and involved in binding to MBD (likely R16-17 based on the length of the segment) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the structural observations and charge complementarity.

claim: Substitution of '848EEGDDT853' with 'NAAIRS' in AnkB led to increased membrane localization presumably due to mutation-induced weakened autoinhibition.
source: This idea is supported by the data from an earlier study showing that substitution of '848EEGDDT853' with 'NAAIRS' in AnkB led to increased membrane localization presumably due to the mutation-induced weakened autoinhibition (He et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Residues from AI-c form extensive hydrogen bonds with the residues in finger loops of ANK repeats.
source: In the AI-c folded-back structure, residues from AI-c form extensive hydrogen bonds with the residues in finger loops of ANK repeats (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Perturbations of hydrogen bonding interactions (e.g. Asn834Lys substitution in AI-c or Asn595Ala mutation in ANK repeats finger loop) led to a few fold decreases in their bindings.
source: Perturbations of these hydrogen bonding interactions (e.g. the Asn834Lys substitution in AI-c or the Asn595Ala mutation in one of the ANK repeats finger loop) led to a few fold decreases in their bindings (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC binding data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Met839 is buried in the hydrophobic pocket formed by Leu668 and Leu701.
source: Hydrophobic interactions also contribute to the AI-c autoinhibition. Met839 is buried in the hydrophobic pocket formed by Leu668 and Leu701; Leu843 interacts with sidechains of Leu597, Tyr630, and Ile635 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Leu843 interacts with sidechains of Leu597, Tyr630, and Ile635.
source: Hydrophobic interactions also contribute to the AI-c autoinhibition. Met839 is buried in the hydrophobic pocket formed by Leu668 and Leu701; Leu843 interacts with sidechains of Leu597, Tyr630, and Ile635 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Individually mutating Met839 or Leu843 to polar Gln weakened the binding by several folds.
source: Individually mutating these two hydrophobic residues to polar Gln weakened the binding by several folds (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC binding data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In epithelial cells, AnkG clusters on plasma membranes whereas AnkB largely localizes to intracellular compartments.
source: In epithelial cells, AnkG clusters on plasma membranes whereas AnkB largely localizes to intracellular compartments (Figure 5A and B and He et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5A and B and citation to prior literature.

claim: Autoinhibition of the MBD by the linker region can modulate AnkB's membrane vs cytosol distributions in epithelial cells.
source: Autoinhibition of the MBD by the linker region can modulate AnkB's membrane vs cytosol distributions in epithelial cells (He et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: WT AnkB mainly localizes in the cytosol, whereas WT AnkG mainly associates with the plasma membranes in polarized MDCK cells.
source: Consistent with the previous report (He et al., 2013), WT AnkB mainly localizes in the cytosol, whereas WT AnkG mainly associates with the plasma membranes in polarized MDCK cells (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: The AnkB 2M and 3M mutants show a higher ratio of plasma membrane localization compared to WT AnkB.
source: We observed that the AnkB 2M and 3M mutants show a higher ratio of plasma membrane localization (Figure 5A and B), consistent with releases of the autoinhibition induced by the two mutations.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: The AnkB ΔLinker deletion mutant (with aa 828–943 deleted) is near completely membrane localized.
source: Finally, we deleted essentially the entire linker region encompassing the complete AI-b and AI-c segments (AnkB ΔLinker, with aa 828–943 deleted), and found that this deletion mutant is near completely membrane localized (Figure 5A and B), suggesting that both AI-b and AI-c can regulate AnkB's membrane localization presumably by modulating its MBD's binding to membrane-anchored target(s).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Both AI-b and AI-c can regulate AnkB's membrane localization presumably by modulating its MBD's binding to membrane-anchored target(s).
source: Finally, we deleted essentially the entire linker region encompassing the complete AI-b and AI-c segments (AnkB ΔLinker, with aa 828–943 deleted), and found that this deletion mutant is near completely membrane localized (Figure 5A and B), suggesting that both AI-b and AI-c can regulate AnkB's membrane localization presumably by modulating its MBD's binding to membrane-anchored target(s).
evidence: This is an inference based on the membrane localization data of the deletion mutant.

claim: Co-expression of NF186 partially recruited WT AnkB to the plasma membranes in HeLa cells.
source: Co-expression of NF186 partially recruited WT AnkB to the plasma membranes (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The 2M, 3M, and ΔLinker AnkB mutants displayed sequentially increasing amounts of NF186-mediated membrane recruitments.
source: The 2M, 3M, and ΔLinker of AnkB mutants displayed sequentially increasing amount of NF186-mediated membrane recruitments in this assay system (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: WT AnkG is better recruited to plasma membranes by NF186 than WT AnkB is.
source: Similar as observed in MDCK cells, WT AnkG is better recruited to plasma membranes by NF186 than WT AnkB is (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: Residues corresponding to the AnkB AI-c are essentially the same in AnkG.
source: Amino acid sequence alignment analysis reveals that residues corresponding to the AnkB AI-c are essentially the same in AnkG, indicating that AnkG also contains an autoinhibitory AI-c segment (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 6A.

claim: AnkG contains an autoinhibitory AI-c segment.
source: Amino acid sequence alignment analysis reveals that residues corresponding to the AnkB AI-c are essentially the same in AnkG, indicating that AnkG also contains an autoinhibitory AI-c segment (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is an inference based on sequence similarity shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The N-terminal half of AnkB AI-b can be aligned with a fragment in the AnkG linker following AI-c, but residues in the C-terminal half of AnkB AI-b that are critical for binding (e.g. Met884 and Tyr886) are missing in AnkG.
source: Curiously, the N-terminal half of AnkB AI-b can be nicely aligned with a fragment in the AnkG linker following AI-c, but residues in the C-terminal half of AnkB AI-b that are critical for its binding to MBD (e.g. Met884 and Tyr886) are missing in AnkG (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Elongating the linker from residue 855 to 903 in the extended AnkG MBD weakened the bindings of Nav1.2, E-cadherin and NF186 to AnkG by 6 ~ 74 folds.
source: Using a similar binding assay developed to discover AI-b in AnkB, we found that elongating the linker from residue 855 to 903 in the extended AnkG MBD (compare aa 38–855 vs aa 38–903) weakened the bindings of Nav1.2, E-cadherin and NF186 to AnkG by 6 ~ 74 folds (Figure 6B), indicating that AnkG linker indeed contains an AI-b segment.
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC binding data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: AnkG linker contains an AI-b segment.
source: Using a similar binding assay developed to discover AI-b in AnkB, we found that elongating the linker from residue 855 to 903 in the extended AnkG MBD (compare aa 38–855 vs aa 38–903) weakened the bindings of Nav1.2, E-cadherin and NF186 to AnkG by 6 ~ 74 folds (Figure 6B), indicating that AnkG linker indeed contains an AI-b segment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the binding data showing that extending the linker weakens target binding.

claim: Direct interaction was detected between AnkG MBD-AI-c protein (aa 38–855) and AnkG's long linker (aa 837–920) or a shorter version of the linker (aa 861–920, lacking AI-c).
source: We also detected direct interaction between AnkG MBD-AI-c protein (aa 38–855, containing the AI-c segment) and an AnkG's long linker (aa 837–920) or a shorter version of the linker (aa 861–920, lacking AI-c) (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC binding data shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: Residues 875 to 903 encompass the complete AI-b of AnkG.
source: Binding affinity-guided mapping revealed that residues 875 to 903 encompass the complete AI-b of AnkG (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC-based mapping data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: AnkG AI-b contains a stretch of highly charged residues in its N-terminal half that are not found in AnkB.
source: It is noted that AnkG AI-b contains a stretch of highly charged residues in its N-terminal half, and these residues are not found in AnkB, revealing a different binding mechanism of AI-b to MBD in AnkB and G.
evidence: This is an observation based on sequence comparison and inference about binding mechanism.

claim: Increasing salt concentrations in the binding buffer significantly weakened the interaction between AnkG_AI-b and AnkG_MBD.
source: We found that increasing salt concentrations in the binding buffer significantly weakened the interaction between AnkG_AI-b and AnkG_MBD, supporting the charge-charge interactions between AI-b and AnkG_MBD (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data (though not shown in the manuscript).

claim: Substituting three charged residues with neutral or charge reverse residues (Asp887Ala, Asp889Ala and Lys890Glu) from the AnkG linker (861-920) completely abolished its ability to bind AnkG_MBD.
source: We substituted three charged residues with neutral or charge reverse residues (Asp887Ala, Asp889Ala and Lys890Glu, indicated with black triangles in Figure 6A) from the AnkG linker (861-920) and found that the mutant completely lost its ability to bind AnkG_MBD (Figure 6F), further supporting the critical roles of the charged residues in AnkG AI-b in its autoinhibition.
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC binding data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: AnkG_AI-b predominantly binds to the 'site-3' of AnkG_MBD.
source: We found that mutations in "site-1' (Phe141Gln, Phe164Gln) or in 'site-2' (Ile277Gln, Leu310Gln) of AnkG_MBD has little effect on AI-b's binding, whereas mutations in 'site-3' (Leu376Gln, Phe409Gln, Leu442Gln) completely abolished the interaction between AI-b and ANK repeats (Figure 6G). This result indicates AnkG_AI-b also chiefly binds to the 'site-3' (repeats R11-14) of AnkG_MBD.
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC binding data with site-specific mutants shown in Figure 6G.

claim: AnkG shares a very similar, three segment-mediated MBD autoinhibitory mechanism as AnkB does, although the AI-b segments in the two ankyrins are different.
source: The above result, together with the findings that AnkG also contains the inhibitory AI-a segment (Figure 1B) and AI-c segment (Figure 6A), collectively demonstrated that AnkG shares a very similar, three segment-mediated MBD autoinhibitory mechanism as AnkB does, although the AI-b segments in the two ankyrins are different.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined biochemical and structural data presented in the study.

claim: Formation of a highly elongated and malleable target binding groove by the 24 ANK repeats with multiple semi-independent target binding sites provides a mechanistic explanation for how ankyrin MBD can bind to many distinct membrane targets with high specificity.
source: Formation of a highly elongated and malleable target binding groove by the 24 ANK repeats with multiple semi-independent target binding sites provides a mechanistic explanation to how ankyrin MBD, via combinatorial usages of its target binding sites, can bind to many distinct membrane targets with high specificity (Figure 7A; and Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on structural and biochemical data, supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The amino acid sequences of all three identified autoinhibitory segments are highly conserved throughout evolution both for AnkB and for AnkG.
source: However, the amino acid sequences of all three identified autoinhibitory segments are highly conserved throughout the evolution both for AnkB and for AnkG, implying that the autoinhibition mechanisms discovered here are evolutionary conserved features for the two ankyrins, respectively.
evidence: This is an observation based on sequence conservation analysis.

claim: The autoinhibition mechanisms discovered are evolutionary conserved features for AnkB and AnkG.
source: However, the amino acid sequences of all three identified autoinhibitory segments are highly conserved throughout the evolution both for AnkB and for AnkG, implying that the autoinhibition mechanisms discovered here are evolutionary conserved features for the two ankyrins, respectively.
evidence: This is an inference based on the high sequence conservation of the autoinhibitory segments.

claim: Disordered sequences tend to evolve more rapidly in eukaryotic genomes.
source: Given that the inhibitory segments of both AnkB and G are intrinsically disordered and disordered sequences tend to evolve more rapidly in eukaryotic genomes (Dyson and Wright, 2005), such high amino acid sequence conservation suggests a strong function-mediated selection against mutational drifts of these inhibitory segments.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The high amino acid sequence conservation of the inhibitory segments suggests a strong function-mediated selection against mutational drifts.
source: Given that the inhibitory segments of both AnkB and G are intrinsically disordered and disordered sequences tend to evolve more rapidly in eukaryotic genomes (Dyson and Wright, 2005), such high amino acid sequence conservation suggests a strong function-mediated selection against mutational drifts of these inhibitory segments.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of high sequence conservation despite the disordered nature of the segments.

claim: The autoinhibitory segments AI-b and AI-c are always retained in all documented AnkB or AnkG variants according to the Ensembl database.
source: However, regardless of the extensive alternative splicing, the autoinhibitory segments AI-b and AI-c are always retained in all documented AnkB or AnkG variants according to the Ensembl database (http://www.ensembl.org), suggesting that the autoinhibitory mechanisms characterized here for AI-b and c are common to all isoforms of AnkB and G.
evidence: This claim is based on database analysis of documented variants.

claim: The autoinhibitory mechanisms characterized for AI-b and AI-c are common to all isoforms of AnkB and G.
source: However, regardless of the extensive alternative splicing, the autoinhibitory segments AI-b and AI-c are always retained in all documented AnkB or AnkG variants according to the Ensembl database (http://www.ensembl.org), suggesting that the autoinhibitory mechanisms characterized here for AI-b and c are common to all isoforms of AnkB and G.
evidence: This is an inference based on the retention of AI-b and AI-c in all documented variants.

claim: The giant AnkG isoforms (270 kDa/480 kDa AnkG) lose the AI-a segment due to alternative splicing.
source: Interestingly, the giant AnkG isoforms (270 kDa/480 kDa AnkG) lose the AI-a segment due to alternative splicing; whereas giant AnkB (440 kDa AnkB) keeps this AI-a segment, suggesting the differential regulation of these giant ankyrin isoforms in nervous systems.
evidence: This is an observation based on analysis of alternative splicing patterns.

claim: Giant AnkB (440 kDa AnkB) keeps the AI-a segment.
source: Interestingly, the giant AnkG isoforms (270 kDa/480 kDa AnkG) lose the AI-a segment due to alternative splicing; whereas giant AnkB (440 kDa AnkB) keeps this AI-a segment, suggesting the differential regulation of these giant ankyrin isoforms in nervous systems.
evidence: This is an observation based on analysis of alternative splicing patterns.

claim: The differential presence/absence of AI-a suggests differential regulation of giant ankyrin isoforms in nervous systems.
source: Interestingly, the giant AnkG isoforms (270 kDa/480 kDa AnkG) lose the AI-a segment due to alternative splicing; whereas giant AnkB (440 kDa AnkB) keeps this AI-a segment, suggesting the differential regulation of these giant ankyrin isoforms in nervous systems.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the differential presence of AI-a in different isoforms.

claim: In AIS, 270 kDa/480 kDa AnkG's SBD exhibits a periodic pattern, while their C-terminus part is not periodically arranged and is found ~32 nm radially deeper than the SBD in the axoplasm.
source: Our data is also consistent with the findings from super-resolution images (Leterrier et al., 2015). In AIS, 270 kDa/480 kDa AnkG's SBD exhibits a periodic pattern, while their C-terminus part is not periodically arranged and is found ~32 nm radially deeper than the SBD in the axoplasm.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior super-resolution imaging study.

claim: AIS AnkG (270 kDa/480 kDa isoforms) lacks AI-a, so the major parts of CT of 270 kDa/480 kDa AnkG are not sequestered by MBD even if AI-b and c are in contact with MBD.
source: AIS AnkG (270 kDa/480 kDa isoforms) lacks AI-a, so the major parts of CT of 270 kDa/480 kDa AnkG are not sequestered by MBD even if AI-b and c are in contact with MBD.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of AI-a in these isoforms.

claim: The 270 kDa/480 kDa AnkG at AIS/Nodes of Ranvier is likely to adopt an open conformation.
source: Furthermore, the 270 kDa/480 kDa AnkG at AIS/Nodes of Ranvier is likely to adopt an open conformation.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the structural and localization data.

claim: The use of multiple semi-independent autoinhibitory segments lining the entire target binding groove of MBD can provide a mechanism for selected release of a few target binding sites while keeping other sites closed.
source: Since each target protein normally occupies a few of the total five proposed binding sites along the entire 24 ANK repeats (Figure 7A), the use of multiple semi-independent autoinhibitory segments lining the entire target binding groove of MBD can provide a mechanism for selected release of a few target binding sites (e.g. sites-1 and 3 for sodium channels) while keeping other sites closed (e.g. site-5), thus allowing selected engagements of MBD to certain target proteins at any given membrane microdomains.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on the structural and biochemical data.

claim: Combinatorial usage of multiple binding sites by target proteins is a rather common strategy for many long repeat-containing proteins.
source: The combinatorial usage of multiple binding sites by target proteins appears to be a rather common strategy for many long repeat-containing proteins (Chook and Blobel, 2001; Conti et al., 1998; Graham et al., 2000; Huber and Weis, 2001; Kobe, 1999; Xu et al., 2010; Zhu et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Autoinhibition of an elongated repeats domain by multiple intrinsically disordered segments from the same protein is rather uncommon, with only a few cases reported.
source: Autoinhibition of an elongated repeats domain by multiple intrinsically disordered segments from the same protein are rather uncommon, and only a few cases have been reported.
evidence: This is a statement about the rarity of this type of autoinhibition mechanism, drawing from knowledge of the field.

claim: Kap60p adopts a somewhat similar autoinhibition mode as ankyrins do, with two NLS recognition sites on the armadillo repeats autoinhibited by two consecutive segments from Kap60p's N-terminal unstructured region.
source: Kap60p, a karyopherin family protein, adopts a somewhat similar autoinhibition mode as ankyrins do. In this case, two NLS recognition sites on the armadillo repeats were shown to be autoinhibited by two consecutive segments from Kap60p's N-terminal unstructured region (Matsuura and Stewart, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Two NLS binding sites of importin-α are inhibited by the same fragment from its N-terminal unstructured region at a 1:2 stoichiometry.
source: In another case, two NLS binding sites of importin-α are inhibited by the same fragment from its N-terminal unstructured region at a 1:2 stoichiometry instead of multiple segments with different sequences as found in ankyrins and Kap60p (Catimel et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The HEAT repeats of karyopherin-β2 are occupied by an internal long loop from the middle region of the HEAT repeats.
source: Other autoinhibition mechanisms found in long repeat-containing proteins include the HEAT repeats of karyopherin-β2 occupied by an internal long loop from the middle region of the HEAT repeats (Chook and Blobel, 1999; Lee et al., 2006a), the HEAT repeats of exportin chromosome region maintenance 1 (CRM1) autoinhibited by a C-terminal α helix immediately following the HEAT repeats (Saito and Matsuura, 2013), and the armadillo repeats of Diaphanous-related formins (Drfs) autoinhibited by a short α helix from its distal C-terminal region (Lammers et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The HEAT repeats of exportin CRM1 are autoinhibited by a C-terminal α helix immediately following the HEAT repeats.
source: Other autoinhibition mechanisms found in long repeat-containing proteins include the HEAT repeats of karyopherin-β2 occupied by an internal long loop from the middle region of the HEAT repeats (Chook and Blobel, 1999; Lee et al., 2006a), the HEAT repeats of exportin chromosome region maintenance 1 (CRM1) autoinhibited by a C-terminal α helix immediately following the HEAT repeats (Saito and Matsuura, 2013), and the armadillo repeats of Diaphanous-related formins (Drfs) autoinhibited by a short α helix from its distal C-terminal region (Lammers et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The armadillo repeats of Diaphanous-related formins (Drfs) are autoinhibited by a short α helix from its distal C-terminal region.
source: Other autoinhibition mechanisms found in long repeat-containing proteins include the HEAT repeats of karyopherin-β2 occupied by an internal long loop from the middle region of the HEAT repeats (Chook and Blobel, 1999; Lee et al., 2006a), the HEAT repeats of exportin chromosome region maintenance 1 (CRM1) autoinhibited by a C-terminal α helix immediately following the HEAT repeats (Saito and Matsuura, 2013), and the armadillo repeats of Diaphanous-related formins (Drfs) autoinhibited by a short α helix from its distal C-terminal region (Lammers et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The membrane target binding groove of MBDs is likely to be closed via autoinhibition during biogenesis and trafficking processes of ankyrins.
source: For example, the membrane target binding groove of MBDs is likely to be closed, via the autoinhibition mechanism elucidated in this study, during biogenesis and trafficking processes of ankyrins.
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional role of autoinhibition during ankyrin biogenesis and trafficking.

claim: Upon reaching each specific membrane domain, certain mechanisms likely exist to release a few selected target binding sites for specific assembly of ankyrin/membrane target complexes.
source: Upon reaching each specific membrane domain, certain mechanisms are likely existing to release a few selected target binding sites for specific assembly of ankyrin/membrane target complexes.
evidence: This is a speculation about the regulation of ankyrin target binding at membrane domains.

claim: The existence of multiple semi-independent inhibitory sequences in the tail of ankyrins suggests that these sequences may be regulated in a combinatorial fashion so that ankyrins can scaffold many different target proteins in different cellular settings and tissues.
source: The existence of multiple semi-independent inhibitory sequences in the tail of ankyrins suggests that these sequence may be regulated in a combinatorial fashion so that ankyrins can scaffold many different target proteins in different cellular settings and in different tissues.
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional significance of multiple inhibitory sequences.

claim: The positioning of the spectrin binding ZZUD domains with respect to the auto-inhibitory sites-a and b suggests a possible spectrin/SBD interaction-induced release of ankyrin autoinhibition.
source: The positioning of the spectrin binding ZZUD domains with respect to the auto-inhibitory sites-a and b suggests a possible spectrin/SBD interaction-induced release of ankyrin autoinhibition.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the spatial arrangement of domains.

claim: Once ankyrins and spectrins meet at specific membrane microdomains, both the bulky ankyrin SBD/spectrin complex and the perceived 'pulling force' exerted by the spectrin-bound SBD may dislodge the two inhibitory segments, AI-a and AI-b, flanking the ZZUD tandem and thus lead to the release of the autoinhibition.
source: Once ankyrins and spectrins meet at specific membrane microdomains, both the bulky ankyrin SBD/spectrin complex as well as the perceived 'pulling force' exerted by the spectrin-bound SBD may dislodge the two inhibitory segments, AI-a and AI-b, flanking the ZZUD tandem and thus lead to the release of the autoinhibition.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic model for how spectrin binding might release autoinhibition.

claim: Ankyrins at AIS/nodes of Ranvier are chiefly 270 kDa/480 kDa AnkG isoforms.
source: Ankyrins at AIS/nodes of Ranvier are chiefly 270 kDa/480 kDa AnkG isoforms.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the ankyrin isoforms present at AIS/nodes of Ranvier.

claim: The 270 kDa/480 kDa AnkG isoforms do not contain the 'AI-a' sequence in their CTs due to alternative splicing.
source: Interestingly, these two larger AnkG isoforms do not contain the 'AI-a' sequence in their CTs due to alternative splicing.
evidence: This is an observation based on analysis of alternative splicing patterns.

claim: The lack of the 'AI-a' site in 270 kDa/480 kDa AnkG means that these two AnkG isoforms can still bind to Nav channels or NF186, albeit with much lower affinities (i.e. a form of semi-open conformation).
source: The lack of the 'AI-a' site in 270 kDa/480 kDa AnkG means that these two AnkG isoforms can still bind to Nav channels or NF186 (See Figure 2B, AnkB 28–965; and also Hedstrom et al., 2008), albeit with much lower affinities (i.e. a form of semi-open conformation).
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of AI-a and binding data.

claim: Spectrin binding to the AnkG SBD may promote further opening of ANK repeats and thus leading to full engagements of the membrane targets of AnkG.
source: Spectrin binding to the AnkG SBD may promote further opening of ANK repeats and thus leading to full engagements of the membrane targets of AnkG.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic model for how spectrin binding affects AnkG conformation.

claim: Membrane targets and βIV spectrin mutually stabilize each other through AnkG at AIS or nodes of Ranvier.
source: Such mutual reinforcement of AnkG-mediated membrane microdomain assembly model is consistent with the findings showing that membrane targets and βIV spectrin mutually stabilize each other through AnkG at AIS or nodes of Ranvier (Yang et al., 2004; Patzke et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The detailed amino acid sequences in the autoinhibitory segments of AnkB and AnkG are quite different.
source: Although AnkB and AnkG share the similar overall autoinhibition modes, the detailed amino acid sequences in their autoinhibitory segments are quite different (Figures 6A and 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence comparison shown in Figures 6A and 7A.

claim: AnkB and AnkG are often targeted to different subdomains in the same tissues including neurons and cardiomyocytes.
source: In parallel with this finding, AnkB and AnkG are often targeted to different subdomains in the same tissues including neurons and cardiomyocytes (Galiano et al., 2012; Lowe et al., 2008; Mohler et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The unique sequences of the inhibitory segments of AnkB and AnkG provide means for them to be differentially regulated.
source: It is possible that the unique sequences of their inhibitory segments provide means for AnkB and G to be differentially regulated.
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional significance of sequence differences.

claim: Post translational modifications such as phosphorylations can provide differential regulation of ankyrins.
source: One such possible mean is via post translational modifications such as phosphorylations (Lu et al., 1985; Cianci et al., 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Ser855 in AI-c, Thr888, Tyr891 in AI-b of AnkG and Thr838, Ser846 in AI-c, Tyr889, Ser890 in AI-b of AnkB can be phosphorylated.
source: We surveyed the PhosphoSitePlus database (http://www.phosphosite.org/) and found that Ser855 in AI-c, Thr888, Tyr891 in AI-b of AnkG and Thr838, Ser846 in AI-c, Tyr889, Ser890 in AI-b of AnkB can be phosphorylated.
evidence: This claim is based on database analysis of phosphorylation sites.

claim: Phosphorylation on some residues within the autoinhibitory segments may lead to differential releases of the MBD autoinhibition of AnkB or AnkG.
source: It is possible that phosphorylation on some of these residues may lead to differential releases of the MBD autoinhibition of AnkB or AnkG.
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential functional role of phosphorylation.

claim: The disordered nature of the autoinhibitory segments of ankyrins is favorable for their accesses to different protein kinases.
source: Again, the disordered nature of the autoinhibitory segments of ankyrins is favorable for their accesses to different protein kinases.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural properties of disordered regions.

claim: Different ankyrin-enriched membrane microdomains (for example AIS) are often selectively enriched with certain protein kinases.
source: It is further noted that different ankyrin-enriched membrane microdomains (for example AIS) are often selectively enriched with certain protein kinases (Bréchet et al., 2008; Hund et al., 2010; Tapia et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.
